title: Continuous Skolem problem
formal: Is there a Turing algorithm that, given any dimension \(d\ge 1\), rational matrix \(A\in \mathbb Q^{d\times d}\), and rational column vectors \(b,c\in \mathbb Q^{d}\), always halts and correctly decides whether \(c^{T}\exp (tA)b=0\) for some real \(t\ge 0\)?
definitions: Every input rational is represented exactly by a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. The dimension is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound. The matrix exponential is \(\exp (tA)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} t^{j} A^{j}/j!\), and \(x(t)=\exp (tA)b\) is the unique real solution of \(x' (t)=Ax(t), x(0)=b\). The target is the hyperplane \(\{x:c^{T}x=0\}; c=0\) is allowed and gives an immediate yes instance. Time ranges over all finite nonnegative real numbers, not just rational or integer times. Equality is exact. A zero at \(t=0\) counts, as does a trajectory that is identically in the hyperplane. If the scalar function approaches zero only in the limit \(t\to \infty\), the answer is no unless it also has a finite zero. No promise of diagonalizability, simple eigenvalues, bounded dimension, stability, spectral separation, transverse intersection, or robust distance from the hyperplane is supplied. The requested algorithm is an ordinary finite-input decision procedure without real-number or number-theoretic oracles; no complexity upper bound is prescribed. This card retains the rational-data version; some cited work treats the more general real-algebraic-data version.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an unconditional always-halting Turing decision algorithm for every finite rational input, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. A positive proof must specify a computable classifier and prove equivalence with \(\exists t\in\mathbb R_{\ge0},\ c^T\exp(tA)b=0\), including tangencies and the initial time. A negative proof must establish undecidability for this exact rational matrix/vector representation. The formalization must cover the analytic semantics and all effectiveness claims, rather than merely postulating an exact real-number test. A conditional procedure assuming Schanuel’s conjecture, a solver for a fixed low dimension, a procedure that may fail to halt, or a certificate requiring a nonzero-distance promise is partial progress. Hardness with arbitrary algebraic coefficients, nonlinear differential equations or a different target set needs a proved reduction into this rational linear model.
why: A minimal exact reachability question for continuous linear systems whose decidability remains unresolved, linking algorithmic verification to real analysis, transcendence and effective number theory.

importance.reason: A fundamental boundary for verification of linear differential systems, with a precisely finite rational input and an unrestricted exact reachability target.

progress.text: Bell and coauthors establish the continuous Skolem framework, equivalent formulations and decidable special cases.
Chonev–Ouaknine–Worrell obtain conditional bounded decidability and reductions for restricted frequency patterns.
Their recurrent-reachability work decides infinitely many zeros at differential order at most seven and supplies effective last-zero bounds in that regime.
Platzer–Qian explain why exact closed-target reachability is not covered by their completeness results for open properties.
The Skolem/Positivity survey records continuous analogues and their distinct analytic obstacles.

Individually rechecked the rational-data target against the 2010 framework, the conditional bounded theorem, the recurrent-zero theorem, the November 2025 exact-target limitation and the July 2026 survey. No matching later resolution was found in a bounded primary-source search.

status_note: The rational linear exact-reachability problem remains explicitly identified as unresolved in the checked November 2025 JACM discussion; the July 2026 survey discusses the continuous analogues and their distinct obstacles. Rechecked through 16 September 2026: no matching unconditional decision procedure or undecidability proof was located. Conditional bounded results, low-order recurrence theorems, open/robust verification and nonlinear or algebraic-coefficient hardness do not by themselves settle this saved rational model. This is a bounded literature review, not proof of continuing openness.

context_blocks.text: Linear differential equations have explicit matrix-exponential solutions, yet an explicit formula does not automatically decide whether a trajectory hits an exact target. The scalar output \(c^{T}x(t)\) may combine growth, decay, polynomial factors and oscillations. The matrix and vectors are finite rational data, while the possible hitting time is an unrestricted real number. This makes the question a basic test of what exact verification can decide even for linear continuous dynamics.

Numerical proximity is insufficient. The one-dimensional system \(x' =- x, x(0)=1\) has output \(e^{- t}\), which becomes arbitrarily small but never reaches zero. Conversely, a zero need not be accompanied by a sign change: the polynomial \((t- 1)^{2}\) touches zero and returns to positive values. Such a polynomial is itself an output of a rational nilpotent linear system. A grid search or a sign-change detector can therefore miss the distinction required by the card.

Simple degenerate cases can be removed exactly. The initial-time condition is \(c^{T}b=0\). By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, the scalar function is identically zero precisely when \(c^{T}A^{j} b=0\) for \(j=0,\ldots ,d- 1\). These are finite rational calculations. Outside that case, analyticity ensures only finitely many zeros in each bounded interval, but neither a uniform numerical precision nor a final time beyond all zeros follows from that finiteness statement.

Spectral decomposition writes the output as a sum of polynomial multiples of exponentials, with conjugate terms combining into real sine and cosine expressions. The imaginary parts of eigenvalues give oscillation frequencies. Repeated eigenvalues can introduce polynomial factors. Competing terms can nearly cancel at very large times, so a proof that the long-term behaviour is simple enough to inspect is a substantive part of an unbounded decision procedure.

Chonev, Ouaknine and Worrell prove decidability of the bounded Continuous Skolem problem assuming Schanuel’s conjecture. That conjecture gives a transcendence-degree lower bound for complex numbers linearly independent over the rationals together with their exponentials. Their algorithm uses it to handle possible tangential zeros. The result does not supply an unconditional bounded-time procedure, and a bounded-time procedure alone does not supply a stopping criterion for checking all \(t\ge 0\).

The same paper reduces certain unbounded spectral cases to the bounded problem, including the case with at most one rationally independent frequency. A separate recurrent-reachability result decides whether a solution of differential order at most seven has infinitely many zeros and gives an effective last-zero bound when it has only finitely many. Combined with the conditional bounded solver, this yields conditional decisions in that low-order regime. Infinite recurrence and existence of even one zero are nevertheless different questions.

The broader algebraic-coefficient formulations reveal a connection with effective Diophantine approximation: handling multiple independent oscillations can entail computing quantities measuring unusually good rational approximations to algebraic numbers. Those implications are evidence of the mathematical obstacles, not undecidability proofs. Their precise dimension thresholds belong to the coefficient model of the cited theorem; this card does not automatically transfer them to the rational-matrix representation fixed above.

Platzer and Qian’s 2025 completeness theorem for compact initial-value problems concerns specified open safety and liveness properties. Its discussion explicitly identifies exact hyperplane reachability as an obstacle to replacing those topological conditions by arbitrary closed targets. A proof system that certifies entry into an open neighbourhood need not decide whether the trajectory touches its central hyperplane. This distinction matters when interpreting advances in numerical verification as progress on exact decision questions.

The July 2026 survey by Bacik and coauthors places the continuous problem alongside discrete recurrence questions, while emphasizing differences in technique. Sampling only integer times gives a sequence but changes the question: for example, a rational rotation system can have output cos t and reach zero at \(\pi /2\). The card asks whether any real hitting time exists, so discrete-time zero testing cannot simply replace the continuous analysis.

sentences: A rational linear differential system evolves as a matrix exponential applied to its initial state.
Continuous Skolem asks whether a specified rational linear observation is exactly zero at some finite nonnegative real time.
The dimension is unrestricted, and the target is an unconditional always-halting Turing decision procedure or an undecidability proof.
Conditional bounded-time and low-order recurrence results do not settle this question, and numerical proximity cannot distinguish a tangency from a near miss.
A resolution would establish a basic limit of exact reachability verification for fully specified continuous linear dynamics.
